honest_take: This is the baseline of modern biking, found on machines meant more for grocery runs than rock gardens. It uses an 7-speed system that works until you look at a steep hill. It is strictly for those who consider "off-road" to be a well-manicured gravel driveway.

This 9-speed groupset is for people who want a mountain bike but mostly use it to fetch bread. It’s significantly heavier than enthusiast gear, but it shifts gears without exploding. Ideal if your idea of "shredding" is accidentally hitting a curb on the way to the pub.

This 9-speed system is built for the casual rider who enjoys having way too many gear combinations to manage. It features a triple chainring at the front, ensuring you have the right gear for every hill and at least five overlapping ones you will never use. It is a workhorse for people who prioritize saving money over saving grams.

This 9-speed drivetrain is for the budget-conscious cyclist who finds the silence of nature overrated. It lacks a clutch, so the chain will slap your frame like a wet noodle every time you hit a pebble. It works, but your bike will sound like a bag of loose silverware going downstairs.

This is the 9-speed drivetrain for the person who doesn't know what "indexing" is and frankly, doesn't want to know. It’s the "Toyota Corolla" of bike parts—it’s not fast, it’s not sexy, and nobody is taking photos of it for Instagram, but it will probably still be shifting (vaguely) when the sun expands and swallows the earth.

This is the cheapest way to put 'Deore' on your bike. It does the job, but without a clutch on the rear derailleur, your chain will sound like loose change in a tumble dryer on rough trails. The price difference goes straight into your beer fund.

This 10 or 11-speed drivetrain is the choice for riders who want the Deore name without the clutter of a modern clutch. It’s significantly cheaper than enthusiast options but leaves your chain free to dance against the frame on every bump. Great for people who find a quiet bike suspicious.

This 11-speed system is for the hobbyist who wants to conquer mountains but still likes having money for pizza. It features a clutch to keep things quiet and a gear range so wide it almost hides the fact that you haven't been to the gym in months. It’s the ultimate "no-shame" workhorse.

This is the cheapest way to get 12 speeds and a clutch that actually keeps your chain on the bike. You’ll need a specific Microspline rear wheel to use it, which is a great excuse to tell your partner why you "absolutely had to" buy new parts. It’s heavy, unpretentious, and works better than your fitness level deserves.

This 11-speed groupset is the blue-collar hero of the trail, offering crisp shifting without requiring a second mortgage. It’s light enough to feel "real" and tough enough to survive your inevitable low-speed tip-overs. It is the perfect choice for riders who prefer riding their bikes to talking about them.

This is essentially the high-end stuff with a heavier coat of paint and significantly less carbon fiber. It offers the full 10-51T range to help you crawl up inclines that would otherwise require a winch. It’s the perfect kit for anyone who realizes that the extra weight of SLX is still lighter than the three beers they had the night before.

This is the drivetrain that made "one-by" conversions mainstream for the rest of us. It shifts with a satisfying, metallic "clunk" that screams quality, even when you're cross-chaining like an amateur. It is the perfect choice for the rider who wants a bike that is objectively better than their actual skill level.

This 12-speed powerhouse is the benchmark for performance that doesn't require a professional sponsorship. It features Hyperglide+ technology, which allows you to shift gears while pedaling like a maniac, without the drivetrain sounding like a car crash. It is the perfect choice for riders who want to win races but still have to pay for their own tires.

This 11-speed masterpiece was Shimano's last stand against the 1x revolution. It’s built with magnesium, carbon, and titanium—basically all the stuff they use to build fighter jets—just so you can shave off the weight of a single granola bar. It shifts with the precision of a Swiss watch, assuming you have the mechanical skills of a Swiss watchmaker to keep it indexed.

The XTR M9100 is for the cyclist who has reached financial enlightenment and decided that spending hundreds of euros to save the weight of a half-eaten banana is a sound investment. It is silent, flawless, and incredibly beautiful—a perfect contrast to the heavy breathing and grunting of the person actually riding it.

The M9050 Di2 is for the cyclist who wants the world to know they have reached "Peak Tech." It’s an incredibly precise system that eliminates human error, meaning the only reason you’re still in the wrong gear is your own brain's failure to process the incline. It is beautiful, expensive, and a great way to experience the unique panic of realizing you forgot to charge your bike before a race.

This 12-speed electronic marvel is for the rider who finds the physical effort of pushing a lever "too taxing." It offers shifting so fast and precise that you’ll run out of excuses for being in the wrong gear before you even realize the hill has started. It’s the ultimate way to spend a fortune to ensure your bike has a better battery life than your phone.

This eMTB only setup is the gateway to the FREE SHIFT and AUTO SHIFT lifestyle. It’s for the rider who wants to be a passenger on their own bicycle, letting the CPU decide which gear is best for their current level of exhaustion. It’s incredibly smart, which is great, because it can finally compensate for your questionable gear choices on steep climbs.

cross_brand_equivalent: SRAM NX Eagle (no wireless equivalent at this price)
honest_take: The M6250 Di2 is for the rider who wants a bulletproof, electronic workhorse that can handle the massive torque of a motor without exploding. It’s heavy, it’s robust, and it removes the last remaining requirement of cycling: thinking. It’s a masterclass in making "difficult" trails feel like a trip to the grocery store, provided you remembered to charge the whole bike.

This is the drivetrain for the rider who loves a challenge—specifically the challenge of keeping a derailleur indexed for more than two consecutive rides. It’s heavy, it’s vague, and the shifter feels like a toy from a cereal box. It’s the ideal setup for someone who wants to learn exactly how to replace a derailleur, because they’ll be doing it very soon.

This is the drivetrain that finally introduced the "Eagle" experience to people who don't want to spend their entire paycheck on a cassette. It uses a standard HG freehub, which is SRAM's way of saying: "We know your old wheels are trash, but you can keep them for now." It shifts okay, but with the subtle finesse of a medieval catapult.

This is the drivetrain for the person who realized that Shimano's shifting was "too smooth" and missed the aggressive, metallic "THWACK" of a gear change that sounds like a gunshot. It features a 520% range, allowing you to climb up vertical walls while your friends with 11-speed setups are busy walking and questioning their life choices.

This 12-speed beauty is for the rider who decided that their bike deserved to be more expensive than their first apartment. It features a carbon cage and a CNC-machined cassette that belongs in a jewelry store window rather than a muddy forest. It’s the perfect choice for the "Enduro Bro" who wants everyone to know they have a high-interest credit card and zero fear of rock strikes.

This is the drivetrain for the rider who believes that if a component isn't Ti-Nitride coated, it’s basically garbage. It’s so light that the wind might actually change your gears for you, and so expensive that you’ll consider putting a GPS tracker inside the derailleur instead of on the frame. It’s the ultimate way to prove that while you can’t buy fitness, you can certainly buy the loudest and most glittery way to fail a technical climb.

This is the drivetrain for the person who is terrible at mechanical maintenance but great at keeping their gadgets charged. It shifts with perfect consistency every single time, assuming you didn't leave the battery on the kitchen counter. It’s an incredible piece of tech that finally allows you to experience the futuristic joy of your gear shifter having a firmware update.

cross_brand_equivalent: Shimano XTR M9150 Di2 / XTR M9100
honest_take: This is for the Enduro rider who wants the ultimate performance and zero cables to snag on branches, but also wants a derailleur that can literally "overload" and move out of the way of an impact. It’s a robotic genius that protects itself better than you protect your own shins. It is the perfect choice for someone who wants to experience the peak of mountain bike tech while simultaneously explaining to their partner why the bike parts cost more than the summer vacation.

This is the ultimate "I have won at life" groupset. It features a titanium-nitride rainbow finish that makes the drivetrain look like it was dipped in liquid stardust and dreams. It’s for the rider who wants 100% wireless perfection and doesn't mind that a single crash could cost them more than a high-end gaming PC. It’s not a bike part; it’s a technological flex designed to make everyone else in the starting grid feel poor.

This is the drivetrain for the person who is tired of "adjusting" things. There are no high/low limit screws, because the computer is now the boss of you. It shifts better the harder you pedal, which is SRAM's way of encouraging you to be an animal on the climbs, or just a way to make sure you wear out your cassette faster. It’s a tank-like piece of machinery that makes your bike look like it’s wearing a robotic prosthetic.

This is the drivetrain for the person who loves "over-engineering." It doesn't just shift; it executes a calculated movement between specifically timed ramps on the cassette, meaning you can shift while pedaling like a maniac and it will still be smoother than your last pick-up line. It is a masterpiece of dark-grey aesthetics, designed for people who want to look professional while they’re actually just struggling to find the trailhead.

This is for the rider who finds the concept of "replacement parts" offensive and prefers "total asset management." It features a carbon cage and the Magic Wheel—a pulley wheel that keeps spinning even if a stick gets jammed in it, because SRAM knows you’re too busy looking rich to notice a branch in your drivetrain. It is the perfect choice for the person who wants the world to know they have reached the final level of the cycling RPG.

This is the drivetrain for the person who has officially completed the "Mountain Biking" video game and is now just playing the side quests in the luxury shop. It is a piece of aerospace engineering that exists because someone at SRAM wondered, "How can we make a derailleur look like a minimalist Italian lamp?" It’s for the rider who wants to feel the trail through their carbon soles but doesn't want to feel the weight of a single extra bolt. It shifts with the cold, unfeeling precision of an AI writing a break-up text—efficient, heartless, and final. It is the ultimate way to turn a bicycle into a high-performance asset that you are genuinely afraid to park outside a grocery store for more than six seconds.
